steps.explanationAfterStep: Hydroxide removes an N–H proton. The negative charge is shared with the carbonyl oxygen (the drawing on oxygen is also accepted).
The anion is brominated on nitrogen: N-bromobenzamide.
The electron-withdrawing bromine makes this N–H easier to remove.

The phenyl group moves from carbon to nitrogen with its bonding pair as bromide leaves: one concerted step, with no free nitrene. The migrating group keeps its configuration. The product is an isocyanate, Ph–N=C=O.

title: Hofmann rearrangement
subtitle: Benzamide, bromine and hydroxide give phenyl isocyanate: a group moves from carbon to nitrogen
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 38

products.caption: phenyl isocyanate + two bromide + two water

reactants.caption: benzamide + bromine + sodium hydroxide
hintTiers: An amide N–H is weakly acidic (pKa about 17), because the anion is shared with the carbonyl oxygen. What does hydroxide do first?
Hydroxide takes one N–H proton; the N–H pair stays on nitrogen. Two arrows.
Hydroxide lone pair → new bond to a drawn N–H hydrogen; that N–H bond → a lone pair on nitrogen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Hydroxide removes a proton from the amide.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Amide hydrolysis needs long heating. Hydroxide acts as a base here: it removes an N–H proton.
Hydroxide and bromine do react, giving hypobromite (BrO⁻), which can also brominate the amide. The route drawn here starts with the amide anion: remove an N–H proton.

amide-anion.caption: benzamide anion + bromine
hintTiers: The amide anion is a nucleophile, and Br₂ is an electrophile. Which atom of the anion makes the new bond?
The nitrogen lone pair bonds to one bromine, and the Br–Br pair goes to the other bromine. Two arrows.
Nitrogen lone pair → new N–Br bond; Br–Br bond → a lone pair on the other bromine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: A second proton is hard to remove from a nitrogen that is already negative. Brominate first: the N–Br compound is more acidic.
The charge is shared with oxygen, but the stable product puts bromine on nitrogen. Bond the nitrogen to bromine.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: nitrogen bonds to bromine. Bromine would then have two bonds: break the Br–Br bond onto the other bromine.

n-bromoamide.caption: N-bromobenzamide + bromide
hintTiers: The bromine on nitrogen makes the remaining N–H more acidic than in the amide. Which base is present?
Hydroxide takes the N–H proton; the N–H pair stays on nitrogen. Two arrows.
Hydroxide lone pair → new bond to the drawn N–H hydrogen; that N–H bond → a lone pair on nitrogen.
n-bromoamide.learnerPrompt: Hydroxide removes the second N–H proton.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Bromide does leave, but from the anion: remove the N–H proton first.

bromoamide-anion.caption: N-bromobenzamide anion
hintTiers: Bromide can leave from nitrogen. Which group on the carbonyl carbon can move onto nitrogen at the same time?
Three arrows: the N–Br bond breaks onto bromine, the phenyl–carbonyl bond moves to nitrogen, and a nitrogen lone pair makes a C=N π bond.
N–Br bond → a lone pair on bromine; bond from the carbonyl carbon to the ring → new bond from the ring carbon to nitrogen; nitrogen lone pair → C=N π bond.
bromoamide-anion.learnerPrompt: The key step: the phenyl group moves to nitrogen as bromide leaves.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Oxygen keeps its C=O. The phenyl group moves to nitrogen, the atom that loses bromide.
Bromide is the leaving group, so the N–Br pair goes to bromine.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right that bromide leaves, but alone that would give an acyl nitrene, with nitrogen short of an octet. The phenyl group moves to nitrogen as bromide goes, and a nitrogen lone pair makes C=N.

mechanismSummary: Hydroxide removes an N–H proton from benzamide, and the anion is brominated on nitrogen. A second deprotonation gives the N-bromoamide anion. As bromide leaves, the phenyl group moves from the carbonyl carbon to nitrogen, giving phenyl isocyanate. In the hot aqueous base the isocyanate goes on to react with water: it adds to the C=N, giving a carbamic acid, which loses CO₂ to give aniline. Overall the amide loses its carbonyl carbon: an amine with one carbon fewer.
